key_provisions_or_claims: A robot tax could offset income tax revenue lost to automation-driven job displacement.
Revenue could fund retraining, reskilling, unemployment benefits and social protection.
Current tax law (e.g. South African Income Tax Act s11D, s12C, s12E, s12BA) favours capital over labour; a robot tax would restore neutrality.
Pigouvian theory frames job displacement and inequality as negative externalities of automation.
Definition of 'robot', double taxation, innovation effects and legal personhood remain unresolved; international coordination is needed.
named_instruments_referenced: EU Civil Law Rules on Robotics 2017
annotation.summary_en: Scoping review (Arksey and O'Malley framework, 15 studies) on robot taxation as a fiscal instrument. It argues a robot tax could offset income tax losses from automation, fund worker retraining, correct capital-over-labour tax bias and reduce inequality, with implications for South Africa and developing economies, while noting definitional and evidence gaps.
annotation.title_clean: Robot taxation as a fiscal policy instrument for sustainable employment: A scoping review with implications for developing economies
annotation.title_en: Robot taxation as a fiscal policy instrument for sustainable employment: A scoping review with implications for developing economies
